qs.q: A 45-year-old woman undergoes imaging for unrelated abdominal pain, revealing a 3 cm incidental liver lesion. Given its suspected diagnosis as the most common benign liver tumor, which of the following diagnostic procedures should be avoided?
qs.e: The most common benign liver tumor is a cavernous hemangioma. Percutaneous biopsy is avoided due to the risk of significant hemorrhage from these vascular lesions.
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - March 7, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman on oral contraceptive pills presents with sudden onset severe RUQ pain and hypovolemic shock. Imaging reveals a ruptured hepatic mass. Which benign liver tumor is most likely?
qs.e: Hepatocellular adenomas are strongly associated with oral contraceptive use and carry a significant risk of spontaneous rupture and life-threatening intraperitoneal hemorrhage.
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - March 7, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 58-year-old female presents with multiple bilateral liver lesions. She has no history of chronic liver disease. What is the most common diagnosis for malignant liver tumors in adults?
qs.e: Metastatic disease (especially from colon, lung, or breast) is far more common than primary liver cancer in non-cirrhotic livers.
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - March 7, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman on oral contraceptive pills presents to the emergency department with sudden onset severe right upper quadrant pain and hypovolemic shock. Imaging reveals a ruptured hepatic mass with significant intraabdominal hemorrhage. Which benign liver tumor is most likely responsible for her presentation?
qs.e: Liver cell adenoma is strongly associated with oral contraceptive use in young women and carries a significant risk of rupture leading to intraabdominal hemorrhage.

qs.q: A 58-year-old female presents with multiple bilateral liver lesions identified on CT scan. She has no known history of chronic liver disease or primary liver tumors. What is the most common diagnosis for malignant liver tumors in adults?
qs.e: Metastatic carcinoma (secondary liver cancer) is the most common hepatic malignancy overall, far outnumbering primary liver tumors.

qs.q: A 2-year-old child presents with an enlarging abdomen and a palpable right upper quadrant mass. Biopsy reveals a malignant epithelial tumor with primitive mesenchymal stroma. Which liver tumor is most commonly seen in this pediatric age group?
qs.e: Hepatoblastoma is the most common primary malignant liver tumor of childhood, typically occurring in very young children.

qs.q: A 65-year-old male with a long history of heavy alcohol use and cirrhosis presents with weight loss and an abdominal mass. His AFP level is 1500 ng/ml. Which primary liver tumor is most likely, and what characteristic differentiates it from Cholangiocarcinoma in this context?
o: Angiosarcoma; typically presents with normal AFP.
Hepatocellular Carcinoma; significantly elevated AFP and association with cirrhosis.
Liver Cell Adenoma; associated with OCP use.
qs.e: Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) is highly associated with cirrhosis from alcohol and presents with significantly elevated AFP. Cholangiocarcinoma is typically associated with normal AFP and different risk factors like PSC.

qs.q: A patient diagnosed with a benign liver lesion is advised against biopsy due to the significant risk of hemorrhage. This contraindication is most characteristic of which benign liver tumor?
qs.e: Cavernous hemangiomas are highly vascular lesions, and performing a biopsy carries a substantial risk of severe, potentially life-threatening hemorrhage.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Liver tumors range from benign hemangiomas to aggressive hepatocellular carcinoma. Diagnosis hinges on imaging, tumor markers, and selective biopsy. Management balances tumor control with liver function and patient comorbidities.

sections.p: Liver tumors are abnormal growths arising from hepatocytes, biliary epithelium, or vascular tissue. Diagnosis starts with imaging; biopsy is reserved for indeterminate lesions.

t.b: Elevated in hepatocellular carcinoma; normal in benign lesions.

sections.p: Staging uses the Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) system for hepatocellular carcinoma, integrating tumor burden, liver function, and performance status.
b: BCLC A: up to 3 nodules <3 cm, preserved liver
BCLC C: portal invasion or extrahepatic spread

sections.p: Risk factors differ by tumor type and region. In low-resource settings, viral hepatitis and aflatoxin exposure dominate.

t.b: High viral load increases hepatocarcinogenesis risk.
Suggests IgG4‑related sclerosing cholangitis, a precursor to cholangiocarcinoma.

sections.p: Symptoms are often nonspecific; many tumors are asymptomatic until advanced.

t.b: Elevated bilirubin and transaminases indicate biliary obstruction or hepatocyte injury.

sections.p: A stepwise approach ensures accurate diagnosis while conserving limited resources.

t.b: Shows arterial phase hyperenhancement and washout, characteristic of HCC.
Reserved for lesions >2 cm with indeterminate imaging; avoids hemorrhage in hemangioma.

sections.p: Certain findings mandate urgent intervention to prevent mortality.

t.b: Detects active bleeding or vascular invasion.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden abdominal pain with hemodynamic instability

faq.a: Risk of massive hemorrhage due to vascular nature.
